newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico ruling party picks veteran for mayor race.
newsitem.headline: Mexico ruling party picks veteran for mayor race.

text.p: Mexico's ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) on Wednesday picked a veteran politician to contest the first-ever elections for mayor of Mexico City in July.

Alfredo del Mazo, who is widely seen as close to the party's old guard, won a crushing victory over two opponents in a vote that the party said was symbolic of its new commitment to democratic procedures.
Del Mazo, 53, won 141 votes of the 189 cast by members of the long-ruling party's Political Council.

Manuel Jimenez, a member of the Mexico City legislative assembly, won 26 votes and Mexico City Attorney General Jose Antonio Gonzalez, seen as the preferred candidate of President Ernesto Zedillo, won 22.
Del Mazo's victory was achieved "without dark accords nor back-room deals," said Roberto Campa, the PRI's leader in Mexico City.
Inhabitants of the Federal District, as Mexico City is formally known, will elect a mayor on July 6. The post has previously been filled by presidential appointment.

The PRI faces a difficult battle to hold on to the mayor's office, with candidates from the leftist Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) and conservative National Action Party (PAN) likely to mount a strong challenge.
The PRI has governed Mexico since 1929 and its old guard is widely seen as reluctant to endorse greater democracy or economic liberalisation.
Del Mazo however pledged a "clean, intense, strong campaign" for the mayor's office.
The Federal District has about nine million inhabitants, while another 10 million people or so live in parts of the capital administered as part of the central State of Mexico.
Del Mazo was the governor of the State of Mexico from 1981 to 1986 and energy minister from 1986 to 1988.
He was one of several candidates to seek the PRI's candidacy for president in 1988 elections but lost out to Carlos Salinas de Gortari, who governed from 1988 to 1994.
Del Mazo has worked his way back to prominence in Mexican politics after committing one of the most spectacular gaffes in the country's recent history.
In 1987 he publicly congratulated a rival of Salinas for winning the PRI presidential candidacy only to find he had got the wrong man. Shortly afterwards he was given a diplomatic post in Belgium.
